tyler_answer:
# Building Product as System Architecture

My work product Building Product as System Architecture 2026-09-11 · By Tyler Lindow Decision In this project, I made a clear decision early on when faced with the option to tell another team to do a database migration or drop a dashboard customers found useful: “ Drop the dashboard. The product is causing these users to do more work. And don't migrate the database. The data schemas are correct. I have found a way for our operations teams to provide this dashboard data and provide more holistic support. ” Context In 2025, I took the lead to bring more cohesion across Partner and Merchant Engineering at Affirm through a merchant-domain architecture review that set which team owns which merchant data. How I led it As the engineering manager overseeing this program, I set up working meetings with every Partner and Merchant Engineering team to enable our tech lead to see around architectural corners only the other tech leads would know about (e.g., are we choosing to consolidate this endpoint or will it become deprecated in a future build?). I also set up kickoff and close meetings with upward and peer leadership to say, “ Work with us! And if you are too busy, tell us. ” Result We got sign-off from 2 Directors, the Principal Architect, and every team's EM, and I presented it to Affirm leadership in Q3 2025. The review showed Merchant Risk and Merchant Advocacy were tightly coupled, which led Affirm to consolidate them under one EM, move former developer-support engineers into SRE, and add PM investment in direct merchant customer problems. Belief Building system architecture is too often seen as simply a requirement to appease the high standards of enterprise customers. System architecture, along with any technical debt work, is always an act of building the core product. “ Are our systems fast enough to get hesitant users to think, 'that was easy' and go tell their friends? ” “ By reducing confusion about data discrepancies in our system, will we grow the bottom line? ” “ If we have another incident, will users leave us, or will they leave us because they just didn't understand how valuable the dashboard was to them? ” Needing operational support isn't a failure, even at a company led by product and engineering. It's how a system grows into something that feels human. Next What Would You Build? Over-Indexing on Intuition in the Age of AI

question: What are you learning about: Building Teams as Raising Funds?
tyler_answer:
# Building Teams as Raising Funds

Building Teams as Raising Funds 2026-09-11 · By Tyler Lindow Decision This work of building teams by raising the funding potential of an individual doesn't happen by mistake, and it also does not happen quickly. Result During my first years as an engineering manager, I promoted a junior engineer to an intermediate position in about 1 year. A few years later, this person moved from support engineering into product-building engineering. And through the span of my time managing this person, they kept getting critical projects over the line and building the organizational intelligence of the team while doing it. Over my tenure at Affirm, my team grew from 1 to 9 engineers, through hiring and 5 engineers who joined through reorgs. How I led it Every week, I checked in with this engineer, giving them a space to process their work challenges and come up with paths forward that aligned with growing the business. Every month, I conducted career growth sessions, giving them a space to consider ways they could invest more in themselves and ultimately in the business. In one particular check-in with this person, I asked, “ What do you see yourself doing in five years? ” And their answer was “ I'd like to become a manager. ” I said, “ Tell me how. ” In similar timing, about six months later, I supported the promotion cycle for another one of my engineers. Belief Raising funds for your position requires an intentional process, and one that is not taken for granted. A goal and a gift. People come and go... but building a team, just like promoting someone, requires constructing a personal belief that: “ I know how to grow this business. ”

question: What are you learning about: Over-Indexing on Intuition in the Age of AI?
tyler_answer:
# Over-Indexing on Intuition in the Age of AI

Leadership opinion What Would You Build? Over-Indexing on Intuition in the Age of AI 2026-08-26 · By Tyler Lindow I think it's product sense. There have been so many times in working with engineers where I tend to be maybe overly empathetic, if that's possible—at least in the context of building a company. But this is one area where I would feel a little frustrated if someone said, “I don't have an opinion about the product.” When I was managing engineering teams at Affirm, the most revealing question I could ask a developer was simply: “What would you build?” Maybe that seems counterintuitive in a corporate context of, “Just tell me what to build.” That last piece of the process we've relied on so much in this industry pre-AI is someone's creative energy. It's the most costly thing—it can get us into rabbit holes, and it can get us into dark places at times because we give so much of ourselves. But it is very important for us to tap into that safely, and use that tool to our advantage in this market. One question to ask yourself is: What does it mean to tap into my creative energy safely? And what does it mean for me to have an opinion about a product? A great place to start is to look at the software products you already love, and figure out why you love them. Dissect them, and reverse-engineer the product a bit. I think that is going to be a critical, must-master skill to survive in this transition into an AI world where the only thing we really have left is what makes us human—what makes us understand when something feels right. That is one of the most valuable things we have left, and so we need to over-index on that and bring that to the forefront as engineers. Previous Building Product as System Architecture

What's confusing is where my third party vendors should be connected to 

Right now I have tinker as my first stop at transforming raw data and then grok bot once my development is declarative.

Right now it's through Cursor builds, and then I view what's in Lindow Labs

question: What are you discovering about what 'good' means to you as an employee that you didn't expect?
tyler_answer:
I’m good being an employee

Well, I see my friend Jon post about his learning and getting a lot of likes on his content and for me my content…

I think I’m a founder and part of me thinks that I just didn’t do it right, like I should have known to do all my outreach from the internet on an internet project

But instead I chose to do all in person outreach 

And connect with people online only after I had met them

And now I’m job searching and getting some traction with companies via cold applications and outreach and it seems to be working…

So I’m learning that my GTM is for being an employee. And just maybe my Foundership journey is for something much more initimate or maybe just not software? It’s hard to say and because I do believe I’ve always had things to say and have tried very hard to say them in multiple ways, but also I am limited by my severance agreement 

In order to lift this curse, I pray 

And maybe all it is finding how I can inspire people still

Opposite, I just kept moving on my internet GTM when I pivoted to job searching

I’m still a founder and I’m still building my approach networking and being comfortable with weak ties
essayTitle: I’m good being an employee

question: When you say the framing of the experience hasn't matured, what specifically are you now noticing that you couldn't see while you were in it?
tyler_answer:
I'm close

I'm closing up my founder story; I realized that it framing and understanding of the experience hasn't matured but that I can do that maturation now.

I want to be perceived as a CEO - one that was not just making architectural decisions and not just spending money will-nilly, but giving it my all

Because I wasn't getting "traction" with new users, I saw my experience as immature. I've even had my own program that I paid for tell me the my experience was immature.

But what's not seen is how dedicated I was - it's the same moment when someone asks "and you're full-time on this?" and I say "yes" and they say "ok wow" in a very serious and intrigued way

It's difficult for people to understand for those that weren't in it when they only see that the outcomes were "small". And sometimes startups make it because they are not just dedicated, but they are pouring more money than they have into, or paying for users to join. My approach was very honest. I extended my work on the company for about 2 months longer than I told myself before I started and that's not something I am proud of. And at the same time, I probably gave up prematurely in the scheme of things. And at the same time I gave up too late because the pivot I made into job hunting was right for me and my business. 

What I want people to understand reading my resume is that this, like so many other startups, are not failures. And at the same time, I did fail to market my product in a way that would gain traction.

There's no way of knowing when to "give up" on your startup, but also if you are honest with yourself and your family, everything will be okay.

I want to let people know that if you take a chance on me, you're getting a future exectutive. I make tough decisions and I make them fast.
